How Does Fox News Frame the WNBA?

Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association

I’ve loved and played (mediocre) basketball all my life, but I only became a real WNBA fan when I moved to Seattle five years ago. (Let’s go, Storm!) Since then, I’ve also become fixated on a question: Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA?

The realization dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t read or watch Fox News myself.

The first clue came at a family gathering while chatting with an older conservative family member. Out of the blue, they started name-dropping WNBA players, praising superstar Caitlin Clark, while making suspect comments about Black players.

This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.

The second clue: my web browser. As I started reading more WNBA news, I was recommended more. That made sense. But then I started getting served coverage from, of all places, Fox News.

Headline after headline pitted the league’s most famous straight white star, Clark, against other WNBA players, mainly Black and/or queer women, like Alyssa Thomas, DiJonai Carrington, or Angel Reese.

When it comes to sports, there are, at least seemingly, facts. This team won, and this team lost. This player scored a lot of points. You would expect a lot of similar coverage. But these headlines were clearly different.

So I decided to collect some data. How does Fox News cover the WNBA compared to everybody else?

Fox News vs. Other Outlets

Mentions in headlines (2020–2026)

Let’s start with online headlines. This chart compares Fox News to other outlets: ESPN, CBS Sports, USA Today, The Athletic, and Just Women’s Sports (read more about how these outlets were chosen in the methodology). If all outlets mentioned Caitin Clark equally, she would be in the middle.

But Fox News mentions Clark 3.2x more than other outlets.

Here’s where the other players stand. Further to the left is more coverage from the other outlets and further to the right is more coverage from Fox

Fox News discusses all-stars like Napheesa Collier, Breanna Stewart, and A’ja Wilson approximately 3-5x less than other outlets…

… and instead gives more coverage to conflict-driven storylines like Sophie Cunningham’s statements about trans athletes,

DiJonai Carrington’s high-profile fouls,

Angel Reese’s animosity toward Clark,

Natasha Cloud’s outspoken activism for BLM, Gaza, and trans rights,

and Brittney Griner’s Russian imprisonment and gender identity.

For years and across topics, Fox News has stoked “hate” and relied on “us vs. them” narratives (Clark vs. Reese), but that playbook didn’t really extend to the WNBA and its players until more recently.

The Fox News-WNBA Expanded Universe

Seven years ago Fox News’ WNBA headlines — like many outlets’ — were few and far between. When they did write about the league, it was for run-of-the-mill events: Cathy Engelbert hired as the commissioner, Sue Bird out with an injury, Napheesa Collier claiming Rookie of the Year honors.

Over time and against a backdrop of Black Lives Matter protests, a second Trump presidency, and a historic CBA, Fox News seized on the expanding league as a culture-war target, framing it as both dangerously radical and illegitimate.

Let’s go back in time to see the evolution.

In 2019, there were barely a handful of Fox News headlines about the WNBA each month. Here, each face is someone Fox News named in a WNBA headline and the size is how often they appeared.

Around 2021 Fox News' coverage begins to drift more political and they start to stage clashes and connections in headlines. Here, a line means two people shared a headline.

They underscored connections between the players’ 2020 BLM activism and then-President Joe Biden, and between point guard Sue Bird (and her then-girlfriend Megan Rapinoe) and Democrats.

They dramatized conflict between Lebron James and Kelly Loeffler, a former WNBA owner and former senator.

In 2021, she was defeated by Democrat Raphael Warnock, in part thanks to WNBA player advocacy.

Then in 2022, Brittney Griner became the central WNBA focal point, because she was arrested and imprisoned in Russia. The league was suddenly imbricated with broader world politics.

After Griner was freed in a prisoner swap, Fox notably turned to Donald Trump to suggest it was a bad deal.

He plainly devalued her life—and so did Fox by consistently airing this framing.

Clark joined the WNBA in 2024 and fully took the spotlight.

She was often pitted against Reese.

To foster animosity between them, Fox News turned to people like Dave Portnoy (Barstool Sports).

After Sophie Cunningham is traded and joins Clark (and Hull) on the Fever to form the “Tres Leches” she becomes the second largest connection in 2026.

At the same time, Fox increasingly platformed anti-trans advocates like Enes Kanter Freedom and Riley Gaines.

This brings us to the summer of 2026 when the right-wing politicization of the WNBA burst into the mainstream.

In July, Sophie Cunningham —Clark’s teammate and on-court “bodyguard”—made anti-trans remarks. While she told ESPN that she “got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans” and clarified that “I never once said that," she also expressed a desire to “protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men"—using the exact language and hateful agenda items of the anti-trans movement. She later doubled down on those comments.

This inspired right-wing politicians and anti-trans advocates around the world to rally around her, including Vice President J.D. Vance, infamous literary TERF J.K. Rowling, and grifter Jennifer Sey.

Trans women’s participation in the WNBA has become a non-stop Fox News talking point. They’ve spent more than 13 hours (!) discussing the WNBA this summer alone. It’s worth repeating: no transgender players are currently in the league.

As Fox News pundit Jesse Watters recently said on air: “We have to do this again, really? Someone wore a t-shirt at a WNBA game? This isn’t a news story…. We don’t even cover the NBA. Why are we covering the WNBA?”

Fightin’ Words

It’s not just the amount of attention that Fox devotes to the WNBA that’s the issue. It’s also the language they use.

To measure this, we’re going to use a method (aptly) called “fightin’ words,” which shows the most distinctive words used by one group vs. another.

Fox News compared with

3,419 Fox articles against 17,016 from all outlets, April 2023 on.

Longer bars are words Fox uses more than other outlets (based on z-scores). Darker bars mean word use is statistically significant (+- 1.96).

Weighted log-odds ratio with an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn 2008), using Jack Hessel's implementation, over headlines from April 2023 on. “All outlets” pools ESPN, CBS Sports, USA Today, Just Women's Sports and The Athletic, which together publish far more than Fox — so the horizontal axis, which counts both archives at once, is mostly theirs. Hover any word for the split. The shaded band is |z| < 1.96, where the difference is not distinguishable from chance.

Here’s how Fox’s vocabulary (right side) differs from other outlets (left side) when reporting on the WNBA. This should look familiar.

You can see Fox’s outsized focus on Clark, Cunningham, Reese, and Carrington...

…and the relative neglect of players like Stewie (Breanna Stewart) or other leading teams (Aces, Liberty).

When we switch to looking at phrases instead of words, you can see the coverage gap between Fox News and other outlets even more.

When we switch to looking at phrases instead of words, Fox consistently uses culture war phrases like ”white privilege” (derogatory) and “biological men” (derogatory, referring to trans women). They talk excessively about hard fouls and players’ comments on social media.

Meanwhile, other outlets talk about the WNBA’s collective bargaining or actual strategy and game play, like free agency, and points and rebounds.

What about language around specific players, like Clark?

This is a juicy question because there is currently a “fight over Caitlin Clark’s soul,” as University of Washington professor Kate Starbird, a leading misinformation researcher and former WNBA player, put it to me.

When Clark joined the league in 2024, the WNBA culture war debates really heated up. Some commentators noted that Clark’s background as a straight, white, Midwestern star may play a role in her broad appeal—a point that conservatives and Fox News pundits have rejected.

But Clark is not a “stable” figure for the conservative or liberal media, Starbird said. And it’s not totally clear what her legacy will be.

One factor in the mix: social media. Starbid has previously written about the increasing pressure athletes feel to take political stances, especially from their large social media audiences. “The real risk for internet influencers—a class of celebrities that increasingly includes professional athletes—isn’t ‘falling down rabbit holes,’ but being ‘captured’ and radicalized by their audiences,” Starbird says. This is a potential risk for everyone from Clark to Cunningham to Carrington and beyond.

The point is that, at least right now, Clark is often talked about more than she talks. And sometimes the conservative media uses her as a pawn for this reason. Let’s take a closer look at the coverage.

How Caitlin Clark is described

Player

Longer bars are words Fox uses more than other outlets (based on z-scores). Darker bars mean word use is statistically significant (+- 1.96).

This is the same “fightin’ words” approach applied per player, and broken down by sentence part. Here, we’re looking at how Clark is described.

Fox News frames Clark as a white phenom, but also as a victim and a target.

Here’s what happens to Clark, according to Fox News.

She is poked, targeted, hit, punched, hip-checked, struck, shoved, and knocked down. She must be protected.

They emphasize her rough treatment much more than other outlets.

Meanwhile, DiJonai Carrington clotheslines, pokes, and hits other players, and commits dangerous fouls.

Both Clark and Carrington play aggressive, but Fox frames Carrington’s play as dangerous and dirty...

while Clark plays hard and phenomenal.

You can see the divergent framing even with specific incidents.

When The Athletic wrote about a play-off game where DiJonai Carrington accidentally poked Caitlin Clark in the eye, for example, they opened by minimizing the incident. They emphasized that Clark herself “downplayed” it, making clear that Carrington didn’t do it on purpose.

By contrast, Fox News opened with a dramatic, descriptive scene of Carrington sticking her “long fingernail” into Clark’s eye, burying Clark’s comments about intentionality paragraphs later.

Flip through the coverage to see more diverging moments, including Fox’s glowing portrayal of Cunningham’s fouls next to their racist description of Alyssa Thomas’s “thug-like play.”

“Rejecting” Identity Politics

Fox News vociferously rejects “identity politics” in WNBA coverage—the reference of social categories like race, gender, or sexuality, and the idea that political issues may be organized around them.

Bobby Burack, writing for Fox’s OutKick, recently criticized ESPN for being “racial idolaters” in their reporting about Clark. There is a false narrative, he claimed, that Clark is only a star “because America has starved for a straight white girl to save them from a league of largely black LGBTQ women.” He concluded: “ESPN ought to add some diversity to its WNBA commentary—diversity of opinion, that is.”

The irony is that Fox News talks more about race, gender, and identity in the WNBA than any other outlet, and much more than ESPN. They’ve mentioned race or racial politics in 21% of their WNBA articles overall, and in 34% this year, compared to just 6% from ESPN.

While LGBTQ+ topics were mentioned less frequently overall, Fox News mentioned them in 13% of WNBA articles overall and in 37% of WNBA articles in 2026 (much of them about trans women’s participation in sports). That’s far more, proportionally, than any other outlet.

Across all the outlets, discussion of race and racial justice peaked in 2020, when WNBA players engaged in highly visible protest in support of BLM. They walked off the court during the national anthem and wore BLM and “Say Her Name” shirts on national television.

But unlike other outlets, Fox News continued to make race a focal point after 2020, especially in relation to “race baiting” and “race bullies” around Clark.

If you look at the words most associated with “race” in Fox’s vocabulary, in fact, it’s race bullies, race idolaters, and race war.

This coverage matters. Many Republican politicians, including Trump, watch Fox News and are often swayed by the reporting. And Fox News is an influential node in a diffuse network of fringe right-wing blogs. According to Open Measures, in the summer of 2026, these right-wing blogs published more than 14,000 posts about the WNBA, and attracted more than 46,000 comments.

Let’s Not Get Played

Fox News has clearly fanned the flames of the WNBA culture war for years—through their emphasis on certain players over (and against) others, through their use of specific coded language, and through their framing of events.

In 2026, Fox discussed the WNBA more than ever, with thirty percent of this coverage mentioning trans athletes or issues. Many of these articles panic over transgender women playing in the WNBA (even though no transgender women are playing in the WNBA).

As Jesse Watters recently said on air, “Why are we covering the WNBA?” Or, more pointedly, “This is something I don’t care about.” He said the quiet part out loud. Fox News doesn’t actually care about women’s basketball. Right-wing pundits and politicians are using the WNBA to push their own agendas.

Of course, sports are political, and they have always been political. Throughout American history, athletes have been able to use their platforms to advocate for justice, and WNBA players are a shining example. In fact, Roxane Gay has argued that the league should step up and match the progressive activism of its players, that it “should lead the charge for making space for trans women in women’s sports.”

Such a move feels, to me, consistent with the spirit of the league. When I went to my first WNBA game, I was shocked by how inclusive it felt. Black, queer, and POC women were celebrated on and off the court, as well on the jumbotron and in the stands. The dancers were teenaged girls doing sick hip-hop moves in baggy pants. The Storm’s adorably goofy mascot, Doppler, uses they/them pronouns. Fox News-types like to make hell of things like that (and, in fact, they have). But the whole vibe was—and is—truly so nice, welcoming, and fun. And the basketball itself is electric. It is completely different from every other professional sporting event I have ever been to.

I don’t know how the WNBA will handle all of this increased attention—from the media, politicians, activists, trolls, new fans, and (unfortunately) my conservative relatives. The new WNBA commissioner certainly has their work cut out for them.

But I know one thing for sure. The version of the WNBA presented by Fox News is not recognizable to me. We need to see this framing for what it is, and push back against it, lest we all get played. Let’s not get played.

Further Reading

  • Katie Barnes. Fair Play: How Sports Shape the Gender Debates. St. Martin’s Press.
  • Jules Boykoff and Ben Carrington. “Sporting Dissent: Colin Kaepernick, NFL Activism, and Media Framing Contests.” International Review for the Sociology of Sport.
  • Letisha Engracia Cardoso Brown, A. Lamont Williams, Amanda N. Schweinbenz, and Ann Pegoraro. “A Perfect Storm: Black Feminism and Women’s National Basketball Association Black Athlete Activism.” Sociology of Sport Journal.
  • Harrison Browne and Rachel Browne. Let Us Play: Winning the Battle for Gender Diverse Athletes. Beacon Press.
  • Courtney M. Cox. Double Crossover: Gender, Media, and Politics in Global Basketball. University of Illinois Press.
  • Mark Falcous, Matthew G. Hawzen, and Joshua I. Newman. “Hyperpartisan Sports Media in Trump’s America: The Metapolitics of Breitbart Sports.” Communication & Sport.
  • Jemele Hill. “What’s Happening to the WNBA Isn’t Normal.” The Atlantic.
  • Sarah J. Jackson. Black Celebrity, Racial Politics, and the Press: Framing Dissent. Routledge.
  • Meghan Kemp-Gee and Megan Praz, eds. Come Out and Play: The Queer Sports Project. Stacked Deck Press.
  • Media Matters. “Fox News Has Spent Over 13½ Hours Waging a WNBA Culture War This Summer.”
  • Open Measures. “A Player’s Anti-Trans Remarks Kicked Right-Wing Attacks on the WNBA into Overdrive.”
  • Ellie Roscher and Anna Baeth. Fair Game: Trans Athletes and the Future of Sports. The New Press.
  • Kate Starbird. “Captured by the Crowd: The Hidden Risk for Athlete-Influencers.” Substack.
  • A. Lamont Williams. “The Heritage Strikes Back: Athlete Activism, Black Lives Matter, and the Iconic Fifth Wave of Activism in the (W)NBA Bubble.” Cultural Studies ↔ Critical Methodologies.

Data & Methods

Headlines and Articles. I collected any Fox News article (both headline and full text) that mentioned the WNBA or its players from 2019-2026. This corpus includes coverage from Outkick, now owned by Fox and published on their site.

As a comparison, I collected parallel WNBA coverage from ESPN, USA Today, CBS Sports, The Athletic (owned by the New York Times), and Just Women’s Sports.

TV Chyrons. I gathered nine years worth of cable news chyrons from Fox, MSNBC, and CNN, drawing on data from the Internet Archive's Third Eye OCR feed, and inspired by a very cool analysis by Charlie Smart.

Players. In this analysis, I include the 30 WNBA players named most in Fox News articles. For the network, I consider individuals named in 10 or more headlines, and add specific politicized individuals like J.D. Vance, Michelle Obama, and Charlie Kirk.

Fightin Words. The word comparisons use “fightin’ words” aka weighted log-odds with an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn 2008).

You can find data and code on GitHub.
